issues.title: Please, no more AI project announcements
issues.body:
There have been more and more announcements of low-effort AI-generated tunnel implementations. The announcements have little value and are becoming distracting and annoying. Please stop posting them.

The purpose of this forum is to aid research and development. What you post here should help increase people's understanding of something—whether it be in the form of documenting censor behavior, analyzing research, or posing an unresolved question you were unable to answer after studying something. "I asked an LLM for a program and this is what it gave me" does not enhance anyone's understanding, even if happens to work practically.

First generating thousands of lines of code and documentation, and only then asking for a review of the design and its assumptions, is doing things backward. Nobody is going to spend time auditing, for free, a mass of code and Markdown files that you did not think about or write yourself—not when the likely outcome is that you'll paste whatever feedback you get into your AI and post what it says as a reply. It must feel gratifying to see a program take shape according to your instructions, but it is not interesting or enlightening for anyone else.

Furthermore, we have no way to evaluate these de novo projects for safety. Users should not volunteer to run new software without at least some assurance that the program and its developers are trustworthy. This applies to both intended and unintended security vulnerabilities: a program may be a trojan horse or may simply be buggy. The fact of LLM development only increases the need for scrutiny, since they are notorious for writing code that appears reasonable on the surface but is weird and convoluted in fact.

There is not much value in posting a bullet list of features and saying "comments welcome". A much better alternative is to make a post about one of the specific *ideas* of your tunnel. Has that idea been used before? Are you combining it with other features in a new way? What makes a new implementation necessary? A good post might be something like: "This is the code that does client authentication. I want it to have properties <var>A</var>, <var>B</var>, and <var>C</var>; I think it does <var>A</var> and <var>B</var>, but how do you also get <var>C</var>?" Or, "I made a table comparing how Shadowsocks, VMess, obfs4, and Drivel do anti-replay; these are the advantages and disadvantages; here is how my implementation does it as a result." Please just write a few reasonable paragraphs in your own words. I am so sick of LLM text.

I am going to close past issues about AI project announcements #589 #634 #635 #649 #665 #669 #673 and will be quicker to close them in the future.

issues.title: OSTP: an AI-assisted Rust tunnel that works in Russia — UDP gets blocked on mobile, real TLS gets through. Looking for review
issues.body:
Yes, this is another AI-assisted protocol (written with a lot of help from
Claude Code). But it works: it gets my relatives through censorship every day
and saves them a fair amount of money and nerves. Now I'd like people who know
DPI better than I do to tell me where the design breaks.

https://github.com/ospab/ostp — AGPL-3.0: the protocol, server, CLI, desktop and
Android apps.

### Wire image

- Handshake: `Noise_NNpsk0_25519_ChaChaPoly_BLAKE2s`; data: ChaCha20-Poly1305.
  Every secret is HKDF-derived from the shared access key. No custom primitives.
- No cleartext version field or magic byte. The 12-byte outer header (session id
  + nonce) is XOR-masked with HMAC-SHA256(obfuscation key, first 32 bytes of the
  packet's ciphertext), so headers are uncorrelated between packets.
- Handshake padding length is drawn from a range derived from the access key, so
  different deployments have different size distributions.
- Optional junk datagrams before the handshake (per-key marker, not a constant)
  and fragmentation of the first TCP write into small chunks.
- An unauthenticated peer gets a fallback website or a decoy, not a reset.

Spec: `docs/en/specification.md`, obfuscation: `docs/en/obfuscation.md`.

### Three carriers for the same datagrams

1. **UDP** — random-looking, own ARQ (selective ACK/NACK) and congestion control.
2. **UoT** — the same datagrams over plain TCP, for networks that throttle unknown UDP.
3. **TLS on 443** (added recently) — UoT inside real TLS with a real Let's Encrypt
   certificate on your domain, directly or behind nginx/Caddy on a secret path.
   Not an imitation: the server is a real website.

### What I've seen in Russia

- **My home (wired) ISP:** almost everything is blocked. OSTP works, and so does
  a carefully tuned VLESS setup; nothing else I tried does.
- **Mobile operators differ a lot.** On MegaFon, one of the biggest, VLESS
  surprisingly isn't blocked, but OSTP over plain UDP and over UoT are blocked
  readily. With UDP the client's counters show only a few hundred bytes coming
  back, and the handshake never completes or the session never becomes stable.
- **TLS works on both** the home ISP and MegaFon.

So in practice the "looks like nothing" carriers are what fails on mobile, and
the real-TLS carrier is what survives.

### What I know is weak

- UDP and UoT are fully encrypted protocols by design, so they're exposed to FEP
  blocking (entropy / "looks like nothing" heuristics) and whitelisting — the
  MegaFon result above is consistent with that.
- Length padding changes sizes but, as far as I can tell, doesn't hide the
  direction/count pattern from #363 (client sends ≥3 packets ≥411 bytes while
  the server talks more often) inside the TLS carrier.
- One developer, no audit.
- The repo has a prober (`ostp-prober`) that tries every carrier against a
  server and estimates where the filtering box is by TTL, but it's rough and
  prints a lot of noise; it needs work before its output is worth sharing.

### Questions

1. The MegaFon UDP case — a few hundred bytes back, then nothing. Does that match
   what others see from TSPU against fully encrypted UDP (the first packets pass,
   then the flow is cut)? Any idea what triggers it: entropy, packet sizes, the
   destination ASN?
2. For traffic carried inside TLS: what inner shaping is actually worth doing
   against encapsulated-handshake fingerprinting?
3. Decoy responses vs silent drop for unauthenticated probes — which one has
   held up better against TSPU's active probing in your experience?


All this message also written by Claude. Sorry about that.

issues.title: core: bound ws/wss/socks handshakes with a dial timeout
issues.body:
## Summary

Only the plain TCP dial is bounded (5 s). After the TCP connection succeeds:

- the WebSocket HTTP upgrade has **no deadline**;
- the WSS TLS handshake has **no deadline** (the default `TLSHandshakeTimeout` of 10 s does not apply because the transport is built by hand);
- the SOCKS negotiation has **no deadline**.

A peer — or middlebox/DPI — that freezes the handshake therefore holds the dial open until the peer is removed entirely, wasting the whole backoff cycle on a dead attempt.

## Fix

Introduce a shared `wsDialTimeout` (15 s, a variable so tests can shorten it) and apply it to each stage:

- `http.Client.Timeout` for the ws/wss upgrade (the websocket library converts it into a context deadline for the whole dial);
- `TLSHandshakeTimeout` for the WSS TLS handshake (not covered by the client timeout);
- a context-bounded SOCKS negotiation via `DialContext` when the proxy supports it (the `x/net` SOCKS5 dialer does).

Files: `src/core/link_ws.go`, `src/core/link_wss.go`, `src/core/link_socks.go`.

## Tests

New frozen-handshake tests (`TestWSDialTimeout`, `TestWSSDialTimeout`, `TestSOCKSDialTimeout`): a server that accepts TCP and never answers; each dial must be abandoned at the timeout (verified: ws 1.00 s, wss 1.00 s, socks 1.00 s with the timeout shortened to 1 s) instead of hanging.

`go test ./src/core/` passes in full (develop + this change).

issues.title: core: honour sni= on WSS dials
issues.body:
## Summary

The WSS dial sets the TLS `ServerName` only from the peering host and ignores the `sni=` peering option that the TLS and SOCKS-TLS links already honour. Peers behind SNI-based virtual hosting (e.g. a WSS endpoint behind an nginx vhost with a real certificate) cannot be reached.

## Fix

Apply `options.tlsSNI` when it differs from the dial hostname, mirroring the other link types. One line block in `src/core/link_wss.go`.

## Test

`TestWSSDialSendsSNI` captures the ClientHello SNI at a TLS listener:

- without the change: SNI carries only the peering host (an IP literal here, so effectively none);
- with the change: SNI carries the `sni=` value.

`go test ./src/core/` passes in full (develop + this change).

issues.title: core: send SNI on QUIC dials and honour sni=
issues.body:
## Summary

The QUIC dial builds a per-host TLS config clone and sets `ServerName` on it — but then passes the **base** config (`l.tlsconfig`, without `ServerName`) to `quic.DialAddr`, so:

- no SNI is ever sent on QUIC dials;
- the `sni=` peering option is silently ignored.

Peers behind SNI-based virtual hosting (shared hosting, CDN, nginx vhosts) are unreachable over QUIC, and the missing SNI makes the dial fingerprintable. The TLS and SOCKS-TLS links already honour `options.tlsSNI`; QUIC and WSS were left out.

## Fix

- Dial with the prepared per-host config instead of the base one.
- Apply `options.tlsSNI` when set, mirroring `link_tls.go`.

One file, four lines changed: `src/core/link_quic.go`.

## Test

`TestQUICDialSendsSNI` captures the ClientHello at a QUIC listener via `GetConfigForClient`:

- without the change: `SNI = ""` (bug reproduced);
- with the change: `SNI = "front.example.org"` from `sni=`.

`go test ./src/core/` passes in full (develop + this change).

issues.title: Fix overflow in tunnel build bandwidth options check
issues.body:
Minimum and requested bandwidth in a tunnel build request are chosen by the builder. The value is read into a uint32_t and multiplied by 1024, so from 4194304 upwards the product overflows: the comparison against the bandwidth limit no longer rejects, and an infeasible demand is accepted. The requested bandwidth branch answers with the requested value instead of the available one for the same reason.

Measured on the real path, with the request record built by the project's own hop config and addressed to the same router. Bandwidth limit 256 KB/s: a minimum of 1 KB/s accepted 10 of 10, a minimum of 100000 KB/s declined 10 of 10, a minimum of 4194304 KB/s accepted 10 of 10. After the fix the last group is declined 10 of 10 and the first is still accepted 10 of 10.

Builds with no warnings, tests pass.

The peer endpoints are resolved with Xray's DNS (resolveLocal), but the UDP
socket for them is dialed with the endpoint string, and DialSystem resolves a
name with the system resolver unless sockopt.domainStrategy is set. With a
name that only Xray's DNS resolves (hosts entries, DoH only setups), the
device never came up: "failed to dial to dest > lookup ...: no such host".

directly. With dialerProxy or finalmask the name is passed on as before, so a

issues.body:
init called device.NewDevice on every call until IpcSet and Up both
succeeded. When one failed (an endpoint name that does not resolve yet, a
socket error), that device stayed alive, and its goroutines kept reading the
TUN shared with the next device. Once a later attempt worked, the leftovers
took part of the outgoing packets. In the new test five failed inits grow the
goroutine count from 100 to 460 on main.

Now the device is created once, and a failed configuration or Up is retried
on the next connection.

issues.title: WireGuard: Use UDP GSO on Linux
issues.body:
With kernel TUN (Linux with CAP_NET_ADMIN, the usual case on servers),
wireguard-go hands Send up to 128 encrypted datagrams of one TSO packet at
once, and the bind writes them with one sendmsg each. Each one then goes
through the UDP/IP stack on its own, so upload costs about twice the CPU of
kernel WireGuard.

Now each run of equal-sized datagrams goes out as one sendmsg with
UDP_SEGMENT, as wireguard-go's own bind does. This is only for a plain UDP
socket: with finalmask or dialerProxy the conn is not one and nothing changes,
and in gVisor mode Send gets one packet per call, so nothing changes there
either. If the kernel rejects UDP_SEGMENT (EIO without checksum offload,
EMSGSIZE or EINVAL when a segment does not fit the path MTU), the bind stops
using it and sends one by one as before.

2 vCPU KVM guest, Linux 6.8, kernel TUN, iperf3 with 4 streams through a
WireGuard server on the internet, Mbit/s:

|                  | upload    | CPU cores per Gbit/s |
|------------------|-----------|----------------------|
| main             | 732-848   | 1.82                 |
| this PR          | 1181-1204 | 0.80                 |
| kernel WireGuard | 1213      | 0.87                 |

Upload on that path tops out near 1.2 Gbit/s, so the CPU column is the better
measure. Download is unchanged (892 vs 902). Behind a VLESS + REALITY inbound
on the same server it looks the same: upload 917-1037 -> 1106-1119 Mbit/s, and
the server's CPU per Gbit/s goes from about 1.5 to 0.8-1.0.

Tests cover grouping datagrams into runs, loopback round trips (IPv4, IPv6,
dual-stack socket to IPv4) with reserved bytes and stats, and the fallback.

fix(dns): fix cache record merge for dual-stack queries on single-family domains
issues.body:
### Problem

In `app/dns/nameserver_cached.go`, `merge()` aggregates resolved records for DNS queries and cache lookups (`queryIP`).

When dual-stack resolution is enabled (`option.IPv4Enable && option.IPv6Enable` -> `mergeReq == true`), the checks on lines 138 and 153 previously evaluated:
```go
if !mergeReq || go_errors.Is(err, errRecordNotFound) {
    return ips, ttl, err
}
```

The `|| go_errors.Is(err, errRecordNotFound)` condition caused unintended early returns whenever either address family had no record:
1. **IPv4-only domains** (or cached records where only `rec.A` is present): `rec4.getIPs()` successfully finds IPv4 IPs, but subsequent evaluation of `rec6.getIPs()` returns `errRecordNotFound`. Line 153 early-returned `nil, 0, errRecordNotFound`, completely discarding the IPv4 addresses collected in `allIPs`.
2. **IPv6-only domains** (or cached records where only `rec.AAAA` is present): `rec4.getIPs()` returns `errRecordNotFound`. Line 138 early-returned `nil, 0, errRecordNotFound`, aborting before `rec6` was ever evaluated.
3. In `queryIP`, this caused valid cached records for single-family domains to be skipped as cache misses (`if !go_errors.Is(err, errRecordNotFound)`).
4. Additionally, `ttl < rTTL` was checked before `len(ips) > 0`, which could overwrite `rTTL` with `0` from a non-existent record.

### Solution

1. Removed `|| go_errors.Is(err, errRecordNotFound)` so that `!mergeReq` solely governs early returns for single-family queries, while dual-stack queries proceed to aggregate available IPs into `allIPs` and record missing errors in `errs`.
2. Updated `rTTL` only when `len(ips) > 0` so non-existent records do not zero out valid TTLs.
3. Returned `ttl = 0` when `len(allIPs) == 0` to align with downstream TTL handling.
4. Added comprehensive unit tests in `app/dns/nameserver_cached_test.go` covering:
   - Single-family IPv4 requests
   - Single-family IPv6 requests
   - Dual-stack requests with both A and AAAA records
   - Dual-stack requests for IPv4-only domains (missing AAAA)
   - Dual-stack requests for IPv6-only domains (missing A)
   - Dual-stack requests when neither record exists

issues.title: Observatory: Fix average RTT overflow on 32-bit platforms
issues.body:
`getStatistics()` computes the average as `time.Duration(int(sum) / cnt)`. `sum` is a `time.Duration` (int64), but `int` is 32 bits on 386/arm/mips/mipsle, so once the samples add up to more than ~2.147 s the sum wraps around. With the default `sampling: 10` that is any outbound slower than ~215 ms.

Seen on a MT7621 router (mipsle, v26.10.10, burstObservatory with leastLoad), `/debug/vars`:

```
"average": -106422465, "min": 304477272, "max": 416019032, "deviation": 430649051
```

The deviation is then computed around that wrong average, and leastLoad sorts by it, so node selection on 32-bit builds is effectively random.

The fix keeps the division in `time.Duration`; it is the same on 64-bit. Running a build with this change on the same router, all averages fall between min and max again and deviations dropped from ~430 ms to 6–132 ms.

The added test documents the case. It passes on 64-bit with or without the fix (CI is 64-bit); with the old code on a 32-bit build, 10 x 400 ms (4e9 ns) wraps to a negative sum, so the average is wrong.

The same line was part of #6237 together with unrelated changes; this PR is only this fix.

issues.title: wireguard, udp: batch TUN/UDP I/O, eliminate hot-path allocations, and fix UDP burst drops & Linux IPv4 routing
issues.body:
## Summary

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    UDPIn["UDP Hub (4096 queue, 7 MiB sockbuf) + Worker (4 MiB pipe, RLock)"] -->|"MultiBuffer"| WGClient["UDPConnClient (AddrPort zero-alloc)"]
    WGClient -->|"gVisor (CUBIC, 4-16 MiB TCP/UDP Buf) / kernelTun (7 MiB sockbuf)"| NetTun["netTun (BatchSize=128, 4096 queue, AsViewList)"]
    NetTun -->|"128-Packet Containers"| WG["wireguard-go Parallel Workers"]
    WG -->|"ReadBatch/WriteBatch (Linux) + 7 MiB sockbuf"| Bind["bind.Send / Receive (BatchSize=128)"]
```

```diff
 proxy/wireguard/
 ├── bind.go / bind_linux.go # BatchSize=128, atomic socket, 7 MiB RCVBUF/SNDBUF (+FORCE), Linux ReadBatch/WriteBatch, UDPAddrPort
 ├── netstack.go             # BatchSize=128, 4096-entry queue, zero-alloc AsViewList read, CUBIC, 4-16 MiB TCP & UDP stack buffers
 ├── client.go               # Move counters to bind; zero-alloc ReadFromUDPAddrPort/WriteToUDPAddrPort in UDPConnClient
 ├── tun.go                  # Comparable udpFlowKey, 4096-pkt queue, 64-pkt batched ReadMultiBuffer, single-view writeRawUDPPacket
 ├── icmp.go                 # Single-view writeRawICMPPacket
 ├── tun_linux.go            # Add missing IPv4 policy routing table/rules + 7 MiB UDP socket buffers
 ├── server.go               # Move traffic counters into bind
 └── *_test.go               # Regression, allocation, and throughput benchmarks
 transport/internet/udp/
 └── hub.go                  # 4096-pkt default hub capacity, 7 MiB UDP socket buffers, zero-alloc WriteToUDPAddrPort
 app/proxyman/inbound/
 └── worker.go               # RLock fast-path for active UDP flows, 4 MiB pipe limit (was 16 KiB / ~13 packets)
```

## Changes

- **`proxy/wireguard/bind.go`, `bind_linux.go`, `bind_other.go`, `client.go`, `server.go`:**
  - Raise `bind.BatchSize()` from `1` to `conn.IdealBatchSize` (`128`), enabling `wireguard-go` to batch up to 128 packets per container across its `runtime.NumCPU()` encryption/decryption goroutines.
  - Set `7 MiB` UDP socket buffers (`SetReadBuffer`/`SetWriteBuffer` + `SO_RCVBUFFORCE`/`SO_SNDBUFFORCE` on Linux when `CAP_NET_ADMIN` is present), matching upstream `wireguard-go`.
  - Remove `PacketCounterConnection` wrapper so `bind` retains direct access to `*net.UDPConn` while accounting uplink/downlink stats per batch.
  - Use pooled `ipv4.PacketConn`/`ipv6.PacketConn` `ReadBatch`/`WriteBatch` (`recvmmsg`/`sendmmsg`) on Linux/Android and `ReadFromUDPAddrPort`/`WriteToUDPAddrPort` across all platforms in both `bind` and `UDPConnClient`.
- **`proxy/wireguard/netstack.go`:**
  - Raise `netTun.BatchSize()` from `1` to `conn.IdealBatchSize` (`128`) and expand `channel.Endpoint` queue depth from `1024` to `4096`.
  - Replace the unbuffered `incomingPacket chan *buffer.View` and eager `pkt.ToView()` clone in `WriteNotify()` with a coalesced `notifyCh` signal and batched draining of `tun.ep.Read()` directly via `pkt.AsViewList()` (0 allocations per read), and release inbound `PacketBuffer` references in `netTun.Write()`.
  - Switch gVisor TCP from Reno (`tcp.NewProtocol`) to `tcp.NewProtocolCUBIC`, enable `TCPModerateReceiveBufferOption(true)`, and set both TCP and stack-level (UDP) send/receive buffer defaults to `4 MiB` (`16 MiB` max) instead of gVisor's `32 KiB`/`212 KiB` UDP defaults.
- **`proxy/wireguard/tun.go`, `icmp.go`:**
  - Replace `map[string]*udpConn` keyed by `src.NetAddr()` with a comparable `udpFlowKey{address, port}` struct (0 allocations per UDP packet lookup).
  - Increase per-flow `udpQueueLimit` from `1024` to `4096` and batch `udpConn.ReadMultiBuffer()` up to `64` packets per call via `popBatch`.
  - Construct raw UDP and ICMP packets in `writeRawUDPPacket` and `writeRawICMPPacket` directly inside a single `buffer.NewViewSize(...)`.
- **`proxy/wireguard/tun_linux.go`:**
  - Add IPv4 routing table allocation (`netlink.FAMILY_V4`), default route (`0.0.0.0/0`), and `AF_INET` policy rules (`Src` and `OifName`) in `createKernelTun`, matching IPv6, and configure `7 MiB` UDP socket buffers on `kernelTun`

issues.title: XDRIVE transport: Add the Google Drive and "template" backend
issues.body:
This stacks on #6745. Until that one is merged the diff here also contains its commit.

### What it adds

A `Storage` implementation for Google Drive, selected with `"service": "Google Drive"`, where `remoteFolder` is a Drive folder id and `secrets` holds ClientID, ClientSecret and RefreshToken.

### No SDK

Plain `net/http`, zero new entries in `go.mod`. It sits behind the same five method `Storage` interface as the local backend, so another provider is one more file and still no dependency.

### How it works

Paths are flattened into single names, so `streams/abc/c2s/000000000.seg` becomes `streams~abc~c2s~000000000.seg`, because Drive has no cheap path lookup and creating nested folders would cost a request per level.

A name to id cache is filled from every listing, so a download costs one request instead of two. The access token is cached and refreshed on expiry or on a 401.

Requests are retried on 429 and 5xx with a jittered backoff capped at 2 seconds. Jitter matters here: at concurrency 32 every request hits the rate limit at the same moment, and synchronised retries only make it worse. A request whose context is already cancelled is not retried at all.

### Measurements

Both ends on a server in the Netherlands, against a real Google Drive account.

Raw storage:

* 4 sequential puts of 256 KiB: 199 KiB/s
* 8 parallel puts of 256 KiB: 1637 KiB/s
* 8 parallel gets of 256 KiB: 2453 KiB/s
* listing a folder of 13 objects: 250 ms
* an uploaded object becomes listable after about 200 ms, so the listing is fresh enough to drive the log

Transport, 10 MB pushed through the WAL:

* segment 128 KiB, concurrency 16: 1187 KiB/s
* segment 256 KiB, concurrency 16: 1513 KiB/s
* segment 256 KiB, concurrency 32: 1849 KiB/s
* segment 512 KiB, concurrency 32: 2111 KiB/s

Real proxy, curl through SOCKS into VLESS over XDRIVE over Google Drive:

* 50 MB in 21.6 s, 2258 KiB/s, about 18.5 Mbit/s, byte identical
* the first byte takes about 2 s, so bulk transfer is comfortable and interactive use is not

Mux, 30 parallel requests, which is roughly one web page:

* without mux: 23675 ms and 30 sessions
* with mux.cool at concurrency 8: 8605 ms and 4 sessions

Stability: 12 of 12 live runs against Drive.

### Tests

A fake Drive server on `httptest` covers upload, listing, download, delete, token caching and retries, and the whole transport is run over it. Live tests against a real account live in the same file and skip unless `XRAY_XDRIVE_DRIVE_SECRETS` points at a credentials file, so nothing here needs secrets in CI.

### Known limits

Credentials sit on the client, so this is for self hosted use. One outbound should enable mux.cool, otherwise every TCP connection becomes its own session with its own files. The HTTP client does not go through Xray's own dialer yet, so `sockopt` and a dialer proxy are not applied to Drive requests.

issues.title: Finalmask noise: Build packets from a Lua script
issues.body:
builds on the lua engine from https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/pull/6823, docs in https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-docs-next/pull/909

-- `noise.script` is a lua script defining `HandleNoise(plan, address)`. it submits each packet with `plan:Send(packet)` or `plan:Send(packet, delay)` for a delay in ms after that packet, and only returns something when it wants to report an error
-- `xray.finalmask.noise` gives the script `Random(size)` for crypto random bytes and `RandomBetween(from, to)`, inclusive. `xray.log` works too. `RegisterLua` exports just those two, so another module's engine can offer them
-- `script` takes whatever #7132 accepts, a path or an inline `base64:` / `base64+gzip:` script, the core resolves it. can't be set together with `noise`
-- this is what `exp` can't do: conditionals, loops, state that survives between calls, and noise that depends on the peer

it follows what the lifecycle page documents for the other pooled hooks: each noise layer gets its own pool so two layers naming the same file don't share state, and a refused return value keeps the instance while only a lua exception or a timeout drops it. the engine is created the first time a layer needs noise, never in infra, which only compiles the script so a typo is caught at startup. the call timeout is 1s rather than 6s because this hook runs while the first packet to a peer waits, the init timeout stays 120s

no LTable on the hook path, one plan per instance that the hook is handed, and the packet buffer is reused per connection

the script only runs when a peer needs noise, never per packet. noise stays best effort: a script that fails only logs a warning and the real packet still goes out, which is how a failed noise write already behaves. sizes, delays and random bounds are capped at 65535 so a script can't ask for a huge allocation or a sleep that never ends

issues.body:
## Summary

```diff
 server TCP dispatch
+  forward request EOF when request copying completes
   keep the response path open until completion or policy timeout
+  release both dispatch pipes and the activity timer on return
 Freedom request copy
+  close the TCP write half after successful copying
```

## Changes

- Forward request EOF in the shared server transport, instead of closing the dispatch writer after response completion. Release both dispatch pipes and the activity timer when `TransportTCP` returns, including abort or cancellation.
- Shut down Freedom's TCP write half after a successful request copy. Statistics unwrapping preserves protocol wrappers, including TLS `close_notify`.
- Add teardown regressions for EOF-dependent responses, buffered requests, delayed responses, reset/cancellation, and statistics-wrapped TCP/TLS connections.

Single-user, multi-user, and relay inbounds use the shared transport. The independent Shadowsocks outbound implementation and native UDP paths are unchanged.

## Project impact

The native regressions below demonstrate request EOF propagation, response preservation, and cleanup on the covered TCP paths. Releasing completed-connection resources is expected to reduce retained memory pressure; the native PR implementation (`d7fdd847`) has no quantified heap benchmark.

### Historical prototype benchmark

A local encrypted SS2022 loopback run compared original historical source at `d2758a0` with an isolated full-lifecycle prototype in the older `singbridge` implementation. This prototype is distinct from the native implementation in this PR. Both variants used Go 1.26.1 on darwin/arm64, 200 generated fixed users, at most 40 live clients, and 1,000 completed connections (5 epochs of 200). Clients closed after sending two 4,096-byte frames to a persistent target; samples were taken after client drain and two forced GCs, without timer acceleration.

| Post-drain metric | Historical original | Corrected prototype |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `HeapAlloc` | 192.67 MiB | 2.08 MiB |
| Goroutines | 6,004 | 4 |
| Active TCP workers | 1,000 | 0 |
| Targets observing request EOF | 0 | 1,000 |

This pair measured approximately 98.9% lower absolute post-drain `HeapAlloc` (202,031,488 vs. 2,180,624 bytes; 1 MiB = 1,048,576 bytes). Both runs completed 1,000 clients without client errors or target deadline events. This percentage applies only to that historical prototype heap sample. It is not a measurement of native PR `d7fdd847`, RSS, cgroup memory, or OOM rate. Forced GC evicts idle pools; arrival jitter differs, and the short run does not establish indefinite leakage beyond existing timers or a throughput/latency improvement.

A separate production trial of the historical backport failed to demonstrate OOM resolution: two additional cgroup OOM kills were observed during the trial, and the original binary was restored. The uncontrolled workload and observations do not establish whether the teardown change caused those events. No production OOM cure or reduction is claimed.

Native implementation regressions:

- **Before:** Added `TransportTCP` regressions failed on missing request EOF and dispatch pipes surviving reset/cancellation. Rebuilt-core single/multi-user cases lost EOF-dependent responses or hit a 5-second peer read deadline with explicit 30-second Xray timeouts.
  **After:** The same tests pass, including complete buffered requests and a final response delayed 150 ms after request EOF.
- **Before:** Real Freedom tests with statistics-wrapped TCP and TLS connections failed while waiting for EOF-dependent responses.
  **After:** Both pass with exact traffic counters; the TLS case verifies `close_notify` without closing the raw TCP write half.

issues.title: TUN: Reassemble fragmented IPv4 and IPv6 input
issues.body:
Valid fragmented IP input never reaches the lightweight TUN stack's transport handlers, even when every fragment fits the TUN MTU. This restores IPv4/IPv6 input reassembly while retaining the single lightweight stack introduced in #7130. That PR explicitly disclosed the omission; this change addresses the supported input case rather than treating it as an undisclosed defect.

At `c77a4d0e4932a53f3eeafafdfef877b56fd660ad`, the IPv4 parser rejects MF/nonzero offsets, and IPv6 Fragment Header 44 reaches no transport handler. Fitting individual IP packets to the MTU does not imply that they are unfragmented.

The reproducer uses a normal local UDP socket in an isolated Linux network namespace, a nonpersistent TUN at MTU 1500, and explicitly permits source fragmentation (`IP_MTU_DISCOVER`/`IPV6_MTU_DISCOVER` set to `DONT`). A 1600-byte payload produces valid IPv4 fragments of 1500/148 bytes and IPv6 fragments of 1496/208 bytes. The same result occurs with plain TUN and with `IFF_VNET_HDR` plus `CSUM|TSO4|TSO6`; fragment coverage and UDP/header checksums were checked. Replaying those unchanged kernel-generated IP packets through production `NewStack` -> `Handler` -> `DispatchLink` gives:

- Previous official `701af607`: IPv4 and IPv6 delivery pass in both modes.
- Current official `c77a4d0e`: unfragmented controls pass, fragmented delivery times out in both modes.
- This patch: both controls and complete fragmented payloads pass in both modes.

Capture and stack replay are separate checks; this is not a claim about every operating system, default socket policy, or network workload.

Reassembly is private to each stack, before existing TCP/UDP/ICMP dispatch. State is bounded to 256 keys including rejection tombstones, a 4 MiB retained-allocation budget (map overhead separately bounded by the key limit), and 256 pieces per datagram. One timer expires entries 60 seconds after first arrival; duplicates do not extend it. Conflicting overlaps reject the datagram through its original deadline, IPv6 atomic fragments are independent, and Close/read failure discard pending state. Unfragmented packets avoid reassembly allocation, clock reads and locks. No public API, configuration or dependency changes are required.

Portable regressions cover packet boundaries/destinations, both fragment arrival orders, duplicate input, IPv6 options before and after the Fragment header, established TCP data, IPv4/IPv6 ICMP echo, invalid input, resource limits, expiry and actual stack lifecycle cleanup. ECN reconciliation, ICMP error generation and output fragmentation remain outside this receive-path change.

Validation with Go 1.27.0:

- Repository formatter: `go run ./infra/vformat/main.go -mode check -pwd ./`.
- Windows/amd64: `go test -race ./proxy/tun/... -count=1`.
- Windows/amd64: all fragment/state tests under `-race -count=3`; lifecycle/allocation additions separately under `-race -count=10`.
- Linux/amd64: `CGO_ENABLED=0` package test binary, then its complete test suite executed on WSL2 kernel `6.18.33.2-microsoft-standard-WSL2`.
- The official-to-official kernel capture/replay discriminator described above, followed by successful replay with the patch.
- Independent parser/resource/lifecycle review and focused review of the added integration tests.

issues.title: TLS ECH: Close connection on failed DoH handshake and slice UDP response
issues.body:
### Summary
This PR addresses connection leaks and buffer handling issues in `transport/internet/tls/ech.go`:

1. **Fix socket leak on failed DoH TLS handshake (`DialTLSContext`)**:
   - In `DialTLSContext`, when establishing the TLS session with `utls.UClient`, if `uConn.HandshakeContext(ctx)` fails (e.g., handshake timeout, connection reset, or TLS negotiation error), the underlying TCP connection returned by `internet.DialSystem` was left unclosed before returning `nil, err`.
   - Now, `_ = conn.Close()` is called upon handshake failure to prevent orphaned TCP socket leaks.

2. **Check error on UDP DNS query write**:
   - `conn.Write(msg)` return value was previously unhandled. We now check `if _, err = conn.Write(msg); err != nil { return nil, 0, err }` to catch write failures immediately.

3. **Correct UDP DNS response buffer slicing**:
   - The UDP response buffer is allocated as 512 bytes. Previously, `dnsResolve = udpResponse` passed the full buffer (including trailing zero padding) to `respMsg.Unpack`.
   - Now correctly sliced to the received byte length: `dnsResolve = udpResponse[:n]`.

4. **Explicit error for unsupported DNS protocols**:
   - Adds an explicit error return (`unsupported ECH DNS server protocol`) when an unsupported DNS server scheme is configured, rather than falling through to unpack a `nil` response.

issues.title: XHTTP: xmux.maxConnections is ineffective in Go 1.27 builds (v26.9.8+, main) — one TCP connection per session while TLS handshakes hang, leading to OOM
issues.body:
### Integrity requirements

- [X] I have read all the comments in the issue template and ensured that this issue meet the requirements.
- [X] I confirm that I have read the documentation, understand the meaning of all the configuration items I wrote, and did not pile up seemingly useful options or default values.
- [X] I provided the complete config and logs, rather than just providing the truncated parts based on my own judgment.
- [X] I searched issues and did not find any similar issues.
- [X] The problem can be successfully reproduced in the latest Release

### Description

> 简述：v26.9.8 起使用 Go 1.27 构建，x/net http2.Transport 改为包装 net/http.Transport。当 TLS 握手被阻断而挂起时，每个会话都会新建一条 TCP 连接，XMUX 的 maxConnections 实际失效，连接数和内存随会话数线性增长。使用 `-tags http2legacy` 构建可恢复正常。与 #6644 不同，这里的额外连接与 MaxConcurrentStreams 无关。

Since v26.9.8 Xray is built with Go 1.27 (`fd2ca748`, "go.mod: Specify Go 1.27.x"); the v26.9.9 release binary reports `go1.27.1`, and the release workflow builds without extra tags. With Go 1.27, `golang.org/x/net` (v0.58.0 in v26.9.9, v0.59.0 on main) compiles `http2/transport_wrap.go`:

```go
//go:build go1.27 && !http2legacy
// Transport wrapping a net/http.Transport.
```

In this mode `http2.Transport.RoundTrip` is delegated to an internal `net/http.Transport` instead of x/net's own `clientConnPool`. The old pool deduplicated in-flight dials per address (`p.dialing[addr]`), so an XMUX client whose handshake hangs held exactly one socket and all further requests waited on it. The new path does not: while no HTTP/2 connection to the host is established yet, every waiting request dials its own TCP connection.

Normally this is invisible — the first handshake completes in one RTT and everything is multiplexed afterwards. But when handshakes hang (e.g. a middlebox blackholes the flow after the ClientHello — the TSPU scenario from #6376), **every proxied session gets its own TCP connection**. `xmux.maxConnections` still limits the number of XMUX clients (the debug log below shows two `XMUX: creating xmuxClient` lines and no removals), but not the dials underneath them.

Consequences:

- `maxConnections: 2`/`3`, introduced as the anti-TSPU default (`18e28390`, #6376), no longer keeps the client under the ~4-connection limit — it opens hundreds or thousands of connections and keeps re-triggering the ban;
- memory grows linearly with hung sessions; in a memory-limited container the process is OOM-killed, taking every other (healthy) outbound down with it.

**Affected:** v26.9.8, v26.9.9 and main (`d562d894`) — all Go 1.27 + x/net ≥ v0.58.0. v26.7.28 and earlier are built with Go 1.26 and use the legacy transport. Tested: XHTTP `stream-one` over TLS (h2). I did not test `packet-up`/`stream-up` or h3.

**Field observation.** Linux client in an LXC container with a memory limit, VLESS + XHTTP `stream-one` + TLS, `maxConnections: 2` (effective config verified with `xray run -dump`, no `extra`). During a TSPU episode against one server (pcap on the router WAN):

- up to **2348** simultaneously open client sockets to that server; bursts of 26 SYNs within 90 ms;
- 1258 of 1261 new connections: SYN/SYN-ACK OK, the ClientHello is never ACKed, retransmitted for minutes;
- the process was OOM-killed twice, 193 s apart (`Memory cgroup out of memory: Killed process ... (xray) ... anon-rss:218772kB`); the healthy HTTP/2 connections of the other outbounds were reset along with it.

Another outbound (different server) in the same process was unaffected — its handshakes complete, so the first HTTP/2 connection is established and everything multiplexes.

**Related**

for https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/pull/6878#issuecomment-6095112915

-- `masqueSettings.xmux`, the same fields and rules as XHTTP. one XMUX connection is one CONNECT-IP tunnel with its own netstack, so maxConnections is the number of tunnels, maxConcurrency and cMaxReuseTimes count flows, and hMaxReusableSecs stops a tunnel from taking new flows and closes it once they are done. hMaxRequestTimes doesn't apply since a tunnel only makes one request. maxConnections defaults to 1 because masque is mostly h3, the other defaults are XHTTP's
-- hKeepAlivePeriod works like in XHTTP: h3 keeps quic-go's 10s, h2 now defaults to chrome's 45s instead of the fixed 10s ping

-- the default tls fingerprint stays: h2 already uses chrome via uTLS, and h3 can't parrot chrome because that means a 1250-byte initial and zero-length connection ids, while masque needs room for 1280-byte packets from the start and warp wants 20-byte ids

I've deleted the message for now. I'm still testing:

1. Approved SHA-256 digests and purposes (DNS/router) are supplied in advance for each core instance. These approvals do not come from subscriptions and cannot be modified by updaters.
2. All bytes read are checked. That same buffer is compiled, without rereading the file.
3. The purpose is supplied by the core's DNS/router code, not by imported JSON.
4. An admitted script always remains sandboxed.
5. Approvals remain immutable while the instance is running. In the initial version, updating or revoking them requires closing the old instance and creating a new one.

Cost and compatibility:

1. Configurations without Lua require no additional steps.
2. Lua users will need initial approval and renewed approval after any file change.
3. An embedding client supplies approvals through the existing `core.NewWithContext`; no shared global approval list is needed.
4. Approval does not make the script itself safe: DNS access, modification of returned data, and resource limits remain separate concerns.

Two separate safeguards are needed:

1. Admission: which code is allowed to execute.
2. Sandboxing: what the running code can do and how many resources it can use.

This proposal addresses the first task.

For example, a client closes its UDP socket and opens a new one with the same source IP:port but a new SessionID. The server's `udpWorker` finds the existing `udpConn` by the source endpoint and continues the same `processUDP` loop. So one `processUDP` invocation cannot be assumed to always correspond to one SS2022 SessionID.

[SIP022 §3.2.4](https://shadowsocks.org/doc/sip022.html#_3-2-4-session-id-based-routing-and-sliding-window-replay-protection) requires servers to route packets by client SessionID rather than source address. An existing session can continue from a different source endpoint, while the same IP:port can later be reused by a new session.

Reproduction for **packet-up over TLS/h2** (the mode the opening post lists as untested), plus a field observation of the impact.

**Setup.** Client: official `Xray-linux-64` builds, **v26.9.9 (go1.27.1)** vs **v26.3.27 (go1.26)**, same config files. Server side: VLESS + XHTTP `packet-up` behind an HTTP reverse-proxy front (CDN-like: terminates TLS, speaks HTTP/1.1 to the origin), client `tlsSettings.alpn: ["h2","http/1.1"]`, uTLS `fingerprint: firefox`. Second target: VLESS + XHTTP `stream-one` over REALITY (direct, no proxy in between). Load: 30 parallel SOCKS sessions (`curl … generate_204` through the client's socks inbound), and I sampled `ss -tnp state established '( dst <entry> )'` every 250 ms filtered by the client's PID. Numbers below are the **peak count of concurrent TCP connections to the entry** during the burst.

| client config (xhttpSettings.extra) | v26.3.27 (go1.26) | v26.9.9 (go1.27.1) |
|---|---|---|
| packet-up, no `xmux` (core default) | 30 | 27 |
| packet-up, `xmux.maxConnections: 3` | 8 | **29** |
| packet-up, `xmux.maxConnections: 1` | 4 | **28** |
| packet-up, `xmux.maxConcurrency: 4` | 14 | 17 |
| stream-one over REALITY, no `xmux` | 29 | 7 |

So with the go1.27 build `maxConnections` has no effect on packet-up either: 30 waiting requests → ~30 dials, exactly as described above. Throughput on a wired link is unaffected (85–115 Mbit/s in every row), the problem is only the number of simultaneous TLS connections.

**Why it matters in the field.** The two mainstream mobile clients in our user base (Happ 6.0.0 iOS/Android and INCY) currently ship core 26.9.9. On Russian cellular networks (tested on T2/Tele2 with the same phone) the packet-up XHTTP entry now behaves like "loads for a moment, then the connection stalls for several seconds, then recovers", while VLESS+Vision entries on the same phone and network work normally; on home Wi-Fi the same XHTTP entry is fine. The same client configs with `maxConnections: 3` / `1` change nothing on 26.9.9, which matches the table. `go.mod` of v26.9.30 and v26.10.10 still says `go 1.27`, so every current release is affected.

Until golang/go#81646 lands, could the release workflow build with `-tags http2legacy` (or could the splithttp dialer de-duplicate in-flight dials itself)? Client app vendors take the official releases as they are, and most users cannot rebuild the core.

comments.body:
I've made some progress here:https://github.com/Ahmad-2213/Xray-core/commits/main/
so far , what i've done with help of AI is:
skip leaf Delete search, bound write concurrency, short List cache; do not hold writer mutex while waiting for upload slot; coalesce concurrent List calls; bound List cache size; one API connection per session; flush first data without coalescing delay; deliver fetched segments in sliding order


Visible improvements are made, though Google Drive is inherently slow, but right now , at least youtube videos can be loaded without buffering & the API consumption is reduced; I'm trying to finalize testing, though some notes I've discovered which is important for API quota management is that mainly , server's upload speed is the client's recieve speed , so most of the upload concurrency should go for server , this will make data transimission asymetric, though it will be more compatible with ADSL setups & also more efficient for Download scenarios.

AI Description:
```
xdrive changes on top of upstream main (7 files, +196/−120), all in transport/internet/xdrive/:

Leaf Delete skips descendant search (drive.go) — before: every Delete ran a List for children, including per-segment deletes; after: names ending .seg/.end/.err return right after deleteID, only session prefixes keep the recursive cleanup.
Bounded write concurrency (wal.go) — before: flushLocked spawned an upload goroutine per segment with the semaphore taken inside upload (unbounded goroutines/PUTs); after: flushLocked acquires w.sem first (same concurrency value, ctx-aware), upload keeps only the release.
No mutex held while waiting for an upload slot (wal.go) — before: w.mu was held across the semaphore wait, stalling writers/flushLoop; after: wg.Add → unlock → wait → spawn → re-lock (cancel path re-locks + wg.Done + ctx err).
40 ms List cache, capped at 256 (drive.go) — before: every poll issued a Drive List; after: per-prefix cache younger than 40 ms is served (copies), random eviction past 256 entries, no invalidation (TTL suffices).
Single-flight List (drive.go) — before: concurrent polls for one prefix issued duplicate Drive queries; after: one leader per prefix via listFlight{done, entries, err} (waiters observe closed done, no result is ever sent on a channel).
First-byte flush without coalescing delay (wal.go) — before: readyToFlush held even the first write up to maxCoalescedTicks ticks; after: data arriving into an empty buffer flushes on the next tick, coalescing still applies to already-buffered growing streams.
Sliding-order segment delivery (wal.go) — before: fetch wg.Wait()ed the whole batch, so one slow Get stalled all later segments; after: per-slot ready channels, each segment is pushed to r.ch as soon as it and all predecessors are ready (strict order kept, ctx-cancel semantics unchanged).
One API connection per session (storage.go, xdrive.go, client.go, drive.go, template.go, drive_test.go) — before: one shared storage/HTTP client for all sessions; after: newSessionConn builds a per-session storage (falls back to listener storage on error, closed in onClose), Close() drains idle conns via new serviceTransport.CloseIdleConnections(); streamConfig nil-guard. Tests: TestDriveSharedClient → TestDriveSessionClients (distinct storages + distinct client RemoteAddrs).
```


**The Only Gain now per AI claim is Higher segment size for lower API operations, This is mostly server side as it plays as the download speed for client.**

172.29.172.254 это Amnezia DNS внутри docker-сети. Новый `freedom` outbound блокирует приватные адреса по умолчанию, поэтому все DNS-запросы клиента уходят в чёрную дыру (см. раздел finalRules в документации Xray: https://xtls.github.io/config/outbounds/freedom.html). В server.json от Amnezia единственный outbound это `{"protocol": "freedom"}` без finalRules.

**Возможное решение**
Добавить в freedom разрешающее правило для адреса Amnezia DNS:

```json
{"protocol": "freedom", "settings": {"finalRules": [{"action": "allow", "port": "53", "ip": ["172.29.172.254"]}]}}
```

Конфиг с таким правилом проходит `xray run -test`. Работу через клиент Amnezia я проверить не смог (мешает другая проблема, см. отдельный issue про fingerprint), так что это предположение, а не подтверждённый фикс.

**Окружение**
- Клиент Amnezia: 5.0.3.0
- ОС клиента: Windows 11 26H2
- Сервер: Ubuntu 22.04, свой VPS, Docker-контейнер amnezia-xray, Xray 26.7.28

issues.title: [Linux] DNS-leak protection blocks LAN DNS — `310.blockDNS` evaluated before `300.allowLAN`
issues.body:
## Summary

With the AmneziaVPN tunnel up, the client firewall rejects **all DNS traffic to LAN resolvers**
(the router, a local Pi-hole, `192.168.x.x`, …). The `300.allowLAN` anchor is clearly intended to
permit local-network traffic, but `310.blockDNS` runs ahead of it, so that intent is unreachable
for port 53.

## Root cause

`client/platforms/linux/daemon/linuxfirewall.cpp`, `LinuxFirewall::install()` (branch `dev`):

```cpp
installAnchor(IPv4, QStringLiteral("320.allowDNS"), {});          // line 216

installAnchor(Both,  QStringLiteral("310.blockDNS"), {            // line 218
                                                            QStringLiteral("-p udp --dport 53 -j REJECT"),
                                                            QStringLiteral("-p tcp --dport 53 -j REJECT"),
                                                        });

installAnchor(IPv4, QStringLiteral("300.allowLAN"), {             // line 222
                                                            QStringLiteral("-d 10.0.0.0/8 -j ACCEPT"),
                                                            ...
                                                            QStringLiteral("-d 192.168.0.0/16 -j ACCEPT"),
                                                            ...
                                                        });
installAnchor(IPv6, QStringLiteral("300.allowLAN"), { ... });     // line 230
```

`installAnchor()` links each anchor's placeholder chain into the root `amnvpn.anchors` chain
**in insertion order** — `installAnchor()` calls `linkChain(..., false)`, which appends with `-A`,
and the placeholder "stays locked into place in the root chain without being removed or recreated,
ensuring the intended precedence order" (comment at `linuxfirewall.cpp:150-152`).

Observed runtime precedence, filter table (`iptables-save`, `amnvpn.anchors`):

```
 1. amnvpn.a.000.allowLoopback
 2. amnvpn.a.320.allowDNS
 3. amnvpn.a.310.blockDNS     <- rejects udp/tcp dport 53
 4. amnvpn.a.300.allowLAN     <- permits 192.168.0.0/16 etc.
 5. amnvpn.a.290.allowDHCP
 6. amnvpn.a.200.allowVPN
 7. amnvpn.a.130.allowMarkedXray
 8. amnvpn.a.120.blockNets
 9. amnvpn.a.110.allowNets
10. amnvpn.a.400.allowPIA
11. amnvpn.a.100.blockAll
```

A DNS query to a LAN resolver (e.g. `192.168.1.1:53`) is REJECTed at step 3 and never reaches
the `-d 192.168.0.0/16 -j ACCEPT` at step 4.

`320.allowDNS` only permits the resolver addresses from the connection profile, and only via the
tunnel interface — so a LAN resolver can never match it:

```
-A amnvpn.320.allowDNS -d 1.1.1.1/32 -o amn0+ -p udp -m udp --dport 53 -j ACCEPT
-A amnvpn.320.allowDNS -d 1.0.0.1/32 -o amn0+ -p tcp -m tcp --dport 53 -j ACCEPT
```

## Evidence — live counters (filter table)

```
amnvpn.310.blockDNS   udp dpt:53  REJECT   320 pkts  24584 bytes
amnvpn.310.blockDNS   tcp dport:53  REJECT     3 pkts    188 bytes
amnvpn.320.allowDNS   1.1.1.1 via amn0+ tcp    337 pkts  27560 bytes
amnvpn.320.allowDNS   1.0.0.1 via amn0+ tcp    225 pkts  18336 bytes
amnvpn.300.allowLAN   192.168.0.0/16 ACCEPT  2792 pkts   351K bytes   <- non-DNS LAN traffic flows
```

The 320 rejected UDP packets are LAN/resolver queries that never left the machine.

## Reproduction

1. Connect with a profile whose `DNS=` points at a public resolver (e.g. `1.1.1.1`).
2. With the tunnel up: `dig @1.1.1.1 example.com` works; `dig @192.168.1.1 example.com` fails.
3. A device on the same LAN with no VPN resolves the same name fine.

## Suggested fix

Move the `310.blockDNS` `installAnchor` call below the `300.allowLAN` calls (both families), so the
LAN allow is evaluated before the DNS block. `320.allowDNS` stays first so the profile's resolvers
keep working:

```cpp
installAnchor(IPv4, QStringLiteral("320.allowDNS"), {});
installAnchor(IPv4, QStringLiteral("300.allowLAN"), { ... });
installAnchor(IPv6, QStringLiteral("300.allowLAN"), { ... });
installAnchor(Both,  QStringLiteral("310.blockDNS"), { ... });   // moved down
```

issues.title: fix: reconnect on Linux only after network is back from suspend
issues.body:
## Problem

On Linux, AmneziaWG has no connectivity after resuming from suspend until the user reconnects by hand.

`LinuxNetworkWatcherWorker::NMStateChanged()` emits `wakeup` when NetworkManager goes to `NM_STATE_ASLEEP` / `NM_STATE_DISABLED`, and `wakeup` is connected to `VpnConnection::reconnectToVpn()`. So the reconnect starts while the machine is **going to sleep**, and the new `activate` reaches the daemon right after resume, when Wi-Fi is not associated yet and there is no default gateway:

```
13:18:47 NetworkManager: sleep requested
13:18:47 LinuxNetworkWatcherWorker : NMStateChanged 10
13:18:47 Reconnect triggered. Reconnecting to the server
13:18:48 kernel: PM: suspend entry (deep)
13:18:55 kernel: PM: suspend exit
13:18:55 NetworkManager state is now DISCONNECTED
13:18:55 Command received: activate
13:18:57 LinuxRouteMonitor : Adding exclusion route for <endpoint>/32
13:18:57 getGatewayAndIface: no gateway found
13:18:57 LinuxRouteMonitor : No default gateway available, skipping exclusion route
13:18:57 WireguardGo : ERROR: (amn0) peer(...) - Failed to send handshake initiation
13:18:57 LinuxRouteMonitor : Adding route to 0.0.0.0/1
13:18:57 LinuxRouteMonitor : Adding route to 128.0.0.0/1
13:18:58 NetworkManager state is now CONNECTED_GLOBAL
13:18:58 LinuxNetworkWatcherWorker : NMStateChanged 70
13:18:58 "Reconnect triggered on Reconnecting during inappropriate state: %2; ignoring slot"
```

The tunnel is up with `0.0.0.0/1` + `128.0.0.0/1` via `amn0` but without the `/32` exclusion route to the endpoint, so the handshake packets are routed into the tunnel itself, and the kill switch blocks everything else. When the uplink does come back (`CONNECTED_GLOBAL`), `networkChanged` is ignored because the connection is still in `Reconnecting`, so nothing repairs the state.

## Fix

Do not reconnect on `ASLEEP` / `DISABLED`; reconnect only on `CONNECTED_GLOBAL`. After resume the connection is still `Connected`, so the `networkChanged` at `CONNECTED_GLOBAL` performs a single reconnect when the default gateway exists, and the exclusion routes are installed normally. `wakeup` is only consumed by `reconnectToVpn()` on Linux, so nothing else is affected. The kill switch keeps `allowDHCP` / `allowLAN` while the old tunnel is still configured, so NetworkManager can bring the uplink back up after resume.

This is the network-watcher part of #2684, without the unrelated firewall / cgroup / routing-table changes (that PR no longer applies to `dev`).

Related: #3037, #2997 (same symptom, exclusion route skipped because there was no gateway at connect time, but triggered by reboot or server switching, which this PR does not address).

## Testing

Reproduced on Fedora 44 (kernel 7.2, NetworkManager, Wi-Fi, S3 `deep` sleep) with AmneziaVPN 5.0.1.5 + AmneziaWG; the log above is from that machine. The fix has not been built locally (no Qt 6 toolchain); relying on CI for the build.

issues.title: [Windows][5.0.3.0] Excluding Weixin.exe via app split tunneling breaks voice/video calls, while text messaging works
issues.body:
## Describe the bug

On Windows 10, excluding `Weixin.exe` (WeChat for Windows) from the VPN using application-based split tunneling causes WeChat video calls to fail.

The VPN connection itself works correctly, and WeChat video calls succeed when application-based split tunneling is disabled or when `Weixin.exe` is not excluded.

After performing six controlled tests (A–F), I found that **adding `Weixin.exe` to the application exclusion list consistently triggers the problem**, while excluding `WeChatAppEx.exe` alone does not.

WeChat TCP connections appear to use the physical Ethernet interface when the main executable is excluded. However, the video call fails, and the observed UDP socket bindings differ from those seen during successful calls.

In some cases, the problem temporarily persists after disconnecting the VPN and fully restarting WeChat.

Important clarification: WeChat text messaging works normally in all tested configurations (A–F). I can send and receive text messages without any issues, even when Weixin.exe is excluded from the VPN. Only voice and video calls fail to connect.

This suggests that the issue specifically affects real-time calling functionality rather than general network connectivity. It may be related to UDP traffic handling, socket binding, or network interface selection, although the exact cause has not yet been confirmed.

## To Reproduce

1. On Windows 10, install AmneziaVPN 5.0.3.0 and connect to a self-hosted VPN server.
2. Disable site-based split tunneling and keep KillSwitch disabled.
3. Enable application-based split tunneling.
4. Select the mode where applications in the list should bypass the VPN.
5. Add `Weixin.exe` to the exclusion list.
6. Connect to the VPN.
7. Completely restart WeChat.
8. Start a new WeChat voice or video call.

**Actual result:** WeChat text messages can still be sent and received normally, but voice and video calls fail to connect or show a call-disconnected message.

**Expected result:** WeChat should use the physical network connection for all required traffic, including video calls, while the VPN remains active for other applications.

## Controlled test results

| Test | VPN | App split tunneling | Excluded WeChat executables | Voice/video calls|
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | Off | N/A | N/A | Works |
| B | On | Off | None | Works |

issues.title: Xray protocol: changing SNI via UI updates `serverNames` but leaves `dest` unchanged, breaking REALITY handshake for strict clients (e.g. sing-box)
issues.body:
### Summary

When changing the SNI field ("Server name (sni)") for the **Xray** protocol via the Amnezia-client UI, the server-side `server.json` inside the `amnezia-xray` container is updated only in `realitySettings.serverNames`. The `realitySettings.dest` field is **not** updated and keeps the original default value (e.g. `www.googletagmanager.com:443`).

As a result, the server continues to fetch and present the TLS certificate of the old `dest` host, while advertising a different SNI to clients. This creates a mismatch between the requested SNI and the returned certificate.

### Affected setup

- Protocol: **Xray (VLESS + REALITY, xtls-rprx-vision)**
- Server: Amnezia self-hosted VPS, protocol installed via Amnezia-client (Docker container `amnezia-xray`)
- Container entrypoint: `dumb-init /opt/amnezia/start.sh`
- Config path inside container: `/opt/amnezia/xray/server.json`
- Clients used for testing: **sing-box 1.14.x** (TUN mode, strict certificate verification), plus Amnezia mobile clients (Android)

### Steps to reproduce

1. Install Xray protocol on a clean VPS via the Amnezia client (Docker container `amnezia-xray`).
2. In the Amnezia client UI, open the Xray protocol settings and change the **"Server name (SNI)"** field from the default value (e.g. `www.googletagmanager.com`) to another domain, for example `files.pythonhosted.org`.
3. Apply changes.
4. On the server, inspect the container config:
   ```bash
   docker exec -it amnezia-xray cat /opt/amnezia/xray/server.json
   ```

### Actual behavior

The config contains a **mismatch**:

```json
"realitySettings": {
    "dest": "www.googletagmanager.com:443",
    "fingerprint": "chrome",
    "privateKey": "...",
    "serverNames": [
        "files.pythonhosted.org"
    ],
    "shortIds": [
        "..."
    ]
}
```

- `serverNames` — updated to the new SNI entered in the UI.
- `dest` — **left unchanged** at the old default (`www.googletagmanager.com:443`).

Because REALITY uses `dest` as the source of the certificate it presents during the handshake, the server returns a certificate valid for `*.google-analytics.com` / `*.googletagmanager.com` while the client expects `files.pythonhosted.org`.

### Expected behavior

Changing the SNI in the UI should update **both** `serverNames` **and** `dest` (or at least provide a separate field / automatic synchronization), so that the presented certificate matches the advertised SNI.

### Impact

- **sing-box** (and any client that strictly verifies the certificate) fails to connect with:
  ```
  x509: certificate is valid for *.google-analytics.com, ..., not files.pythonhosted.org
  ```
- Amnezia mobile clients appear to work because they do not strictly verify the returned certificate, which **masks the bug** during normal use.
- The mismatched SNI/certificate pair is an anomaly in TLS traffic that can be flagged by DPI systems, potentially putting the server IP at risk of being blocked.

### Workaround

Manually editing `dest` inside the container fixes the issue:

```bash
docker cp amnezia-xray:/opt/amnezia/xray/server.json /root/server.json
# edit "dest" to match "serverNames", e.g. "files.pythonhosted.org:443"
python3 -m json.tool /root/server.json > /dev/null && echo "JSON OK"
docker cp /root/server.json amnezia-xray:/opt/amnezia/xray/server.json
docker restart amnezia-xray
```

However, this is fragile: any subsequent change to the Xray protocol via the Amnezia client UI (adding a client, changing SNI, etc.) overwrites `server.json` and reverts `dest` back to the old default, requiring the manual fix again.

### Suggested fix

In the Amnezia-client code that generates `server.json` for the Xray protocol, when the user changes the SNI, update `realitySettings.dest` accordingly (e.g. set `dest` to `<new_sni>:443`), or add an explicit `dest`/`target` field in the UI so both values can be configured and kept in sync.

### Environment

- Amnezia-client version: _5.0.3.0_
- Desktop OS: Windows 11
- Server OS: Debian 13

issues.title: feat(client): add opt-in reconnectable QUIC connection pool
issues.body:
## Summary

Related to #1431. Add an opt-in QUIC connection pool to the core API and client YAML; existing constructors and defaults remain unchanged.

```yaml
quic:
  connectionPoolSize: 2
```

Values 1..8; omitted or 0 means one connection. Applies to client proxy/forwarding/TPROXY/TUN modes; Realm pooling is rejected. Share URIs and the single-stream speedtest command stay unchanged.

- Sizes 2..8 use independent reconnectable QUIC connections; size 1 preserves the existing path.
- Assign new TCP streams and UDP sessions round-robin. Established flows stay on their member; no single-stream bonding or replay.
- Split nonzero bandwidth targets statically, preserving the aggregate target. This is not a shared wire-rate limiter.
- Serialize config/callback execution and handle initialization failures and concurrent close.

## Validation

Full Linux `core`/`app` and serial `extras` tests, formatting and changed-package vet passed. Pool and CLI config-to-client tests passed `-race -count=20` on Linux and Windows, including real TCP/UDP, defaults and invalid sizes, eager/lazy startup, fragmentation and member recovery.

Three paired MT7981 runs measured download median **271 -> 349 Mbps (+28.4%)**, with higher CPU use. One pooled run reported **0.58% loss and UDP memory errors**; this is not a long-term stability claim. Method and limits: [benchmark](https://github.com/rison1337/hysteria/blob/feat/optional-connection-pool/CONNECTION_POOL_BENCHMARK.md).

## Before merge

- **Depends on #1696** for retired-transport cleanup. A [separate validation branch](https://github.com/rison1337/hysteria/tree/test/pool-reconnect-cleanup) passed repeated real server-restart/recovery checks with that fix.
- API shape and static Brutal allocation policy need maintainer agreement.
- Upstream CI still requires approval to run the fork workflow.

No server/protocol, quic-go, router or overclock changes are included. AI-assisted; locally reviewed and tested.

issues.title: Multiplex Controller (Bypass connection-based speed limit)
issues.body:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**
Hy2 makes only 1 multiplexed connection for all client's sub-connections, in the cases that speed of each connection is limited, performance of Hy2 is also limited.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
Hysteria2 can add option to make a connection pool and do a load-balance, or make a new connection when the last connection has N sub-connections.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
\-

**Additional context**
\-

comments.body:
I have a working experimental client-side connection-pool prototype and some measurements relevant to this request. Would maintainers be interested in an **opt-in pool of reconnectable QUIC connections** for CPU-constrained clients?

The motivation in my case is client-side processing throughput, not bypassing a server/account bandwidth policy. New TCP streams and Hysteria UDP sessions are assigned round-robin; each returned TCP stream / UDP session stays on its original connection. This is not multipath and does not bond a single stream.

### Small paired experiment

Cudy WR3000S / MT7981, two Cortex-A53 cores, OpenWrt 25.12.5, Linux 6.12.94. The CPU was held at **1640 MHz in both cases**; these are not stock-clock results. Windows Ookla CLI on a wired LAN client, through router TPROXY, same VPN server and same Speedtest server (50771, Frankfurt). Three tests per case, alternating A/B, on 2026-10-04:

| Metric | 1 QUIC connection | 2 QUIC connections |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Download median | 273.32 Mbps | 368.22 Mbps |
| Upload median | 290.08 Mbps | 284.60 Mbps |
| Download loaded latency median (Ookla IQM) | 216.96 ms | 110.49 ms |
| Mean of per-run loaded CPU means | 73.82% | 87.36% |
| Process RSS maximum across runs | 69.59 MiB | 69.36 MiB |
| MemAvailable minimum across runs | 45.48 MiB | 47.33 MiB |

The download median increased by approximately **34.7%**. The six download samples were 263.09 / 276.58 / 273.32 Mbps for one connection and 368.22 / 368.22 / 364.76 Mbps for two.

### Important qualifications

- Both A and B used the same experimental Hysteria/quic-go binary. UDP GRO and receive-buffer recycling were enabled in **both** cases, as were `GOMEMLIMIT=64MiB` and nice -5. This isolates pool size within that prototype, but is **not** a stock-upstream-versus-pool-only benchmark.
- Brutal's configured bandwidth targets were kept at an aggregate **450 Mbps down / 300 Mbps up** by dividing the targets evenly among connections. This is a static allocation, not a shared rate limiter: a single stream cannot borrow idle members' allocations. Loss compensation and server-side per-connection policies still need review; dividing targets is not proof of correct aggregate congestion behavior.
- Kernel UDP buffer-error counters and WAN drop counters did not increase during these six runs. However, diagnostic QUIC receive-queue drops remained: 33,855 across A and 65,791 across B. External DIRECT ICMP probes also missed replies (3/68 and 7/66, respectively, with a short 500 ms timeout). I am **not** claiming zero packet loss or proven long-term stability.
- A separate three-repeat 2-versus-3-connection experiment produced 356.97 versus 367.75 Mbps download medians, only about 3% improvement. More connections are not automatically better.
- The prototype is based on Hysteria 2.12.3 and a local quic-go fork based on `v0.62.1-0.20260912175848-73339f7edbb9`. A submission would need rebasing and testing with the current pinned dependency.

If this direction is welcome, I would propose a small, separate pool-only PR: default size 1 / existing behavior unchanged, explicit configuration rather than experimental environment variables, documented static bandwidth allocation, per-session affinity, and tests for lazy/eager initialization, cleanup, reconnect and concurrent close. GRO, receive-path changes and OpenWrt/overclock/guard scripts would not be included.

In particular, would you prefer to restrict the initial pool feature to an automatically controlled congestion mode, or consider static per-connection Brutal target allocation if the limitations are explicit? I would appreciate guidance before settling the public API/configuration shape.
